subject: Reasoning
description: Two-premise syllogisms with possibility / either-or conclusions

questions.stem: Statements: 'All birds are animals. All animals are living things.' Conclusion that follows necessarily:

options.option_text: Some animals are not birds, definitely true
All birds are living things by transitivity
All living things are animals, fully true
Some living things are not birds either

questions.explanation: Standard categorical transitivity: All A are B; All B are C → All A are C. Birds → animals → living things; therefore all birds are living things. Distractor 1 may be true factually but doesn't FOLLOW from the premises (premises don't say there are non-bird animals). Distractor 3 reverses the implication. Distractor 4 again may be true but not strictly entailed.

questions.stem: Statements: 'Some pens are pencils. All pencils are erasers.' Which conclusion follows?

options.option_text: All pens are erasers, fully true
Some pens are erasers, by overlap
All erasers are pens, fully true
No pen is an eraser, fully true

questions.explanation: Some pens are pencils → those pen-pencils are also erasers (since all pencils are erasers). So SOME pens are erasers. Cannot conclude ALL pens are erasers. Distractor 1 too strong. Distractor 3 reverses 'all'. Distractor 4 contradicts.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem: Statements: 'No cat is a dog. Some dogs are pets.' Which conclusion follows?

options.option_text: All pets are dogs, true universally
Some pets are not cats, true necessarily
No pet is a cat, true universally
All cats are pets, true universally

questions.explanation: Some dogs are pets → those dog-pets exist; no cat is a dog → those dog-pets are not cats. So SOME PETS ARE NOT CATS. Distractor 1 too strong (premises don't say all pets are dogs). Distractor 3 too strong — there COULD be cats that are pets too. Distractor 4 is unrelated and unsupported.

questions.stem: Statements: 'All teachers are educated. All educated people read books.' Which conclusion follows?

options.option_text: All readers are teachers, true universally
All teachers read books, by transitivity
Some teachers don't read, true sometimes
Only educated people are teachers ever

questions.explanation: Transitivity: teachers → educated → readers. So all teachers read books. Distractor 1 reverses the chain. Distractor 3 contradicts the universal. Distractor 4 mistakes 'all teachers are educated' for the converse 'only educated are teachers' — these are different.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem: Statements: 'Some books are heavy. All heavy things are difficult to lift.' Which conclusion follows?

options.option_text: All books are difficult to lift, true
Some books are difficult to lift, true
Heavy things are always books only
Difficult to lift implies it is a book

questions.explanation: Some books are heavy + all heavy things are hard to lift → those heavy books are hard to lift → SOME books are hard to lift. Distractor 1 too strong. Distractor 3 reverses. Distractor 4 also reverses.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem: Statements: 'No flower is a fruit. Some flowers are red.' Which conclusion follows?

options.option_text: All red things are flowers necessarily
Some red things are not fruits necessarily
No red thing is a fruit necessarily
All fruits are red things necessarily

questions.explanation: Some flowers are red. No flower is a fruit → those red flowers are not fruits → SOME RED THINGS are not fruits. Distractor 1 too strong (red things include other categories). Distractor 3 too strong — non-flower red things could be fruits. Distractor 4 unsupported.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem: Statements: 'All squares are rectangles. Some rectangles are red.' Which conclusion follows?

options.option_text: All squares are red, fully true
Some squares may or may not be red
No red figure is a square, fully true
All red things are squares, fully true

questions.explanation: Some rectangles are red — but those red rectangles might or might not include any squares. The premises don't FORCE any square to be red. Conclusion: cannot conclude either 'some squares are red' as DEFINITE. Often expressed as 'possibility' — squares may or may not be red. Distractor 1 too strong. Distractor 3 unsupported. Distractor 4 reverses.
